title: Egypt's regions · GeoClick Geography
edition: Regions of Europe · one lesson per country · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Egypt's regions, part 1 of 1. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
We work through 27 of the Egypt regions the map names, once each: where it sits, one fact worth keeping, and a hook to remember it by.

states.name: Damietta
lines: Damietta stands on the Mediterranean coast at the mouth of the Damietta branch of the Nile, at the north-east corner of the delta, with Dakahlia inland to the south.
The Fifth Crusade besieged this port for eighteen months and took it in 1219, and Francis of Assisi crossed the siege lines here to meet the sultan.
Remember the Delta port that held out for a year and a half against a crusade, and that still builds most of the country’s furniture.

states.name: Kafr el-Sheikh
lines: Kafr el-Sheikh covers the northern edge of the Delta between Gharbia to the south-west and Dakahlia to the south-east, reaching the Mediterranean shore between the two branches of the Nile, and its name means the sheikh’s village.
Its Burullus lagoon is one of the great wetlands of the Delta and a stopping point on the migration route between Europe and Africa, and almost all of it is farmland of rice and cotton.
Remember the sheikh’s village on the Delta’s northern shore, with the lagoon where European and African birds meet.
states.transition: Let's bring Kafr el-Sheikh into view.

states.name: Port Said
lines: Port Said stands on the Mediterranean at the northern entrance of the Suez Canal, on the narrow strip of land north of the waterway, with Al Sharqia to the west and Sinai across the canal to the east.
It was a free port for decades, so Egyptians came here to buy imported goods when nowhere else in the country had them, and the Anglo-French invasion of 1956 landed on the same frontage.
Remember the northern gate of the canal, the free port that stocked the whole country, and the beach where the invasion of 1956 came ashore.
states.transition: Let's bring Port Said into view.

states.name: Dakahlia
lines: Dakahlia fills the heart of the Delta, between Damietta to the north and Qalyubia to the south, with the Damietta branch of the Nile running down through it and Mansoura as its capital.
Mansoura is where Louis IX of France was held prisoner in 1250, so his crusade ended in a house in this town, and the governorate is one of the most productive farming ones in the Delta.
Remember the Delta governorate whose capital was a prison for a French king, and whose name comes from a village nobody has heard of.

states.name: Gharbia
lines: Gharbia is the western half of the Delta, lying between the Rosetta and Damietta branches of the Nile and well inland from the sea, with Tanta in the middle.
Mahalla al-Kubra in it is Egypt’s textile town, and its mill strikes fed straight into the uprising of 2011, while Tanta’s festival for al-Sayyid al-Badawi draws crowds the size of the Hajj.
Remember the western Delta, where the mills lit the uprising of 2011 and the great festival is said to rival the Hajj.

states.name: Alexandria
lines: Alexandria sits on the Mediterranean at the western edge of the Delta, with Beheira inland to the east and Matrouh along the coast to the west, and the city fills almost the whole governorate.
Alexander the Great founded and named it in 331 BC and laid it out himself, and its library was the largest in the ancient world, while its lighthouse has long since toppled.
Remember the city Alexander laid out on the Mediterranean shore, whose lighthouse has fallen and whose royal quarter now lies under the harbour.

states.name: Al Sharqia
lines: Al Sharqia is the eastern Delta, running from the edge of the Delta near Cairo out towards Port Said and Ismailia, with Zagazig as its capital and the Damietta branch of the Nile separating it from Dakahlia to the west.
Bubastis here was the cult city of Bastet, the cat goddess, and Herodotus called her festival the rowdiest in Egypt, and the governorate is the country’s largest producer of oranges.
Remember the eastern Delta, the cat goddess’s festival town, and the orange groves that supply most of the country’s fruit.
states.transition: Let's bring Al Sharqia into view.

states.name: Beheira
lines: Beheira is the broad western Delta governorate on the Mediterranean between Alexandria and Kafr el-Sheikh, reaching inland to the desert edge near Giza and Matrouh, with Damanhur as its capital.
Rashid, the old Rosetta, is here, and it was there in 1799 that a French soldier found the Rosetta Stone, the key that unlocked hieroglyphs.
Remember the wide green Delta governorate whose name means lake, holding the stone that unlocked hieroglyphs.

states.name: Ismailia
lines: Ismailia sits on the isthmus between the Mediterranean and the Gulf of Suez, east of Cairo and north of Suez, with the canal running along its southern edge.
Lake Timsah, a natural lake in the middle of it, is the one the canal was routed through, and the town was named for the khedive who built the canal and bankrupted Egypt doing it.
Remember the canal town with villas and wide avenues, and the natural lake the canal had to cross.

states.name: Monufia
lines: Monufia is a small Delta governorate inland to the south of Tanta, hemmed between Gharbia, Qalyubia and Beheira, with Shibin el Kom as its capital.
It has no desert at all, every square metre is Delta farmland, and two Egyptian presidents, Sadat and Mubarak, were both born in this small governorate.
Remember the small all-farmland Delta governorate that produced two presidents and has not a grain of desert in it.

states.name: North Sinai
lines: North Sinai fills the flat northern half of the Sinai peninsula, from the Mediterranean at El Arish down to the Gulf of Suez, facing the delta coast across the water.

The coastal road across it was the invasion route between Egypt and Asia for four thousand years, walked by armies in both directions, and its Bedouin tribes speak a dialect closer to the Levant than to the Nile.
Remember the flat northern half of Sinai, the invasion road along its shore, and the Bedouin dialects that lean towards the Levant.
states.transition: Let's bring North Sinai into view.

states.name: Qalyubia
lines: Qalyubia is the narrow governorate just north of Cairo, wrapping around the apex of the Delta where the Nile splits, with Benha as its capital.
The Delta Barrages here, begun in 1843, were the first great modern attempt to control the Nile’s flow, and the governorate is now effectively Cairo’s northern suburb.
Remember the strip of farmland north of Cairo, where the Delta Barrages first taught Egypt to hold back the river.

states.name: Cairo
lines: Cairo sits at the apex of the Delta where the Nile divides, with no sea at all, hemmed in by Giza across the river to the west and Qalyubia to the north.
Al-Qahira means the victorious, and it was named in 969 for the planet Mars, which was rising in the sky when the Fatimids laid the foundations.
Remember the capital named for the rising planet Mars, standing exactly where the river chooses to split.

states.name: Matrouh
lines: Matrouh is the long north-western governorate, running from the Mediterranean above Alexandria inland across the Libyan desert to the borders of Giza and the New Valley, with Matruh on the coast.
Egypt’s longest stretch of Mediterranean coast is here, with water clear enough to look Caribbean, and El Alamein nearby holds about twelve thousand war graves in three cemeteries.
Remember the long desert coast above Alexandria, with the clearest sea in Egypt and the battlefields of 1942 behind it.

states.name: Suez
lines: Suez stands at the southern end of the canal where it opens into the Gulf of Suez, north of the Red Sea governorate and south of Cairo, with desert on both sides.

The canal opened in 1869 and cut the voyage from London to Bombay by about seven thousand kilometres, and it needs no locks because the Mediterranean and the Red Sea sit at effectively the same level.
Remember the lockless canal at the foot of the country, where the sea is at the same height at both ends.

states.name: Faiyum
lines: Faiyum is an oasis basin on the west side of the Nile valley, south of Giza and north of Beni Suef, with the river fed into it by a channel dug in the Middle Kingdom.
Lake Qarun in it is a remnant of a far larger lake, and its Fayum mummy portraits, painted on wood in the Roman period, are the most lifelike faces to survive from the ancient world.
Remember the green basin inside the desert that the Nile feeds by hand, and the painted wooden faces staring out of its tombs.

states.name: Beni Suef
lines: Beni Suef is a governorate of the middle Nile valley on the west bank of the river, south of Faiyum and Giza and north of Minya, with desert closing in on both sides.
At Meidum here a pyramid partly collapsed, leaving a tower standing inside its own rubble, which shows how the shape was worked out, and the governorate is a major producer of cement.
Remember the sons of Suef on the middle river, with the pyramid that fell down on itself and left the answer in the rubble.
states.transition: Let's bring Beni Suef into view.

states.name: Giza
lines: Giza is the great governorate on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, running from the Delta in the north down through the desert past the pyramids, with Giza city at its heart.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest building in the world for about 3,800 years, longer than anything else has ever held the record, and the Sphinx beside it is carved from a single ridge of limestone.
Remember the west bank with the oldest tallest building on earth, and the Sphinx cut from the quarry ridge that was left behind.

states.name: South Sinai
lines: South Sinai is the mountainous southern half of the Sinai peninsula, between the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba, with El Tur as its capital on the shore.
St Catherine’s monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai has been occupied continuously since 565 and holds the second largest collection of early manuscripts after the Vatican.
Remember the mountain half of Sinai, with the oldest working monastery in the world and the deep Blue Hole off its reefs.
states.transition: Let's bring South Sinai into view.

states.name: Minya
lines: Minya is in the middle of the Nile valley, north of Asyut and south of Beni Suef, with the river running through it and the desert hills of the Red Sea governorate close on the east.
Amarna is here, the city Akhenaten built in a single reign for his one-god religion and abandoned immediately after his death, and the governorate has the largest Christian share of any in Egypt.
Remember the bride of Upper Egypt, the most Christian of the governorates, with the empty city of the one-god king on its edge.

states.name: Asyut
lines: Asyut is on the middle Nile, north of Sohag and south of Minya, with the valley narrow and the desert hills pressing close on the east.
Its name comes from Ancient Egyptian Zawty through Coptic Siout, meaning guardian, because it guarded the caravan route that ran forty days to Darfur.
Remember the guardian town that watched the caravan road south for forty days to Darfur.

states.name: Sohag
lines: Sohag is on the middle Nile between Asyut to the north and Qena to the south, with the river valley narrow and the western desert closing in beside it.

Abydos here was the cult centre of Osiris and holds the king list that gave Egyptologists their chronology, and the red and white monasteries nearby are among the oldest Coptic buildings still standing.
Remember the governorate with Osiris’s shrine and the king list that dated the pharaohs, and the two fifth-century monasteries nearby.

states.name: Luxor
lines: Luxor is a small governorate on the middle Nile, carved out of the old Qena governorate and lying just to the north of it, holding the temples of Karnak on the east bank and the tombs of the west bank opposite.
The Greeks called it Thebes and the Arabs al-Uqsur, the palaces, and Tutankhamun’s tomb was found here in 1922, the only royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings discovered nearly intact.
Remember the narrow strip of temples and tombs where the boy king’s tomb was found, and the columns of Karnak.

states.name: Qena
lines: Qena sits on the middle Nile between Sohag to the north and Luxor to the south, with the river bending sharply east around the city and the Red Sea governorate’s border to the east.
The Qena bend is where the Nile swings sharply east, the sharpest turn in its whole course, and Dendera’s temple of Hathor here had its ceiling zodiac carved in the last years of the Ptolemies.
Remember the sharpest bend in the Nile and the temple ceiling zodiac that ended up in the Louvre.

states.name: Red Sea
lines: The Red Sea governorate is the long eastern strip along the shore of the Red Sea, running from the Gulf of Suez down past Hurghada to the border with Sudan.
The sea it takes its name from is one of the saltiest in the world and the only one with no river flowing into it, and these reefs carry some of the highest coral cover on earth.
Remember the long eastern shore with the saltiest sea and no river at all, and the reefs scientists are watching as the water warms.
states.transition: Let's bring Red Sea into view.

states.name: New Valley
lines: New Valley is the vast desert governorate of the far south-west, running from the edge of the Nile valley near Qena and Asyut out to the Libyan border, with the Kharga oasis in it.

It is the largest governorate in Egypt, about forty-four per cent of the country, with well under one per cent of its people, and its oases sit over one of the largest bodies of fossil water on earth.
Remember the giant empty governorate that is nearly half the country for less than one per cent of the people.
states.transition: Let's bring New Valley into view.

states.name: Aswan
lines: Aswan is the southernmost governorate on the Nile, below Qena and west of the Red Sea, where the river runs through desert to the Nubian frontier.
Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth using a well here in about 240 BC and got within a few per cent, and the High Dam of 1970 ended the Nile flood and created Lake Nasser.
Remember the southern frontier town where a well proved the size of the Earth, and the dam that tamed the river’s flood.

recap: 27 regions of Egypt, one for each target of the map: Damietta, Kafr el-Sheikh, Port Said, Dakahlia, Gharbia, Alexandria, Al Sharqia, Beheira, Ismailia, Monufia, North Sinai, Qalyubia, Cairo, Matrouh, Suez, Faiyum, Beni Suef, Giza, South Sinai, Minya, Asyut, Sohag, Luxor, Qena, Red Sea, New Valley and Aswan.
Remember the shape of Egypt from the inside: the regions nest around each other, and every name on the map belongs somewhere in this one country.
